Monday night his convoy left Brasília and split four ways while reporters chased the wrong cars; Tuesday his allies told the press he was already in Florida while he was still in Brazil, driving hundreds of miles to the triple frontier.

At 10:50 p.m. he crossed the bridge into Puerto Iguazú with his wife and daughters, Argentine airport police escorted him to a Gulfstream that Trump adviser Jason Miller had helped charter, Milei's top aide watched from the ground in contact with Eduardo Bolsonaro, and the plane lifted off at 12:21 a.m. with Flavio flying on his Italian passport, refueled in Ecuador, and landed at Opa-locka at 9:30, where officers shielded the family with umbrellas.

October 29, 1618. Walter Raleigh asked to inspect the axe before they used it on him, ran his thumb along the edge, and said it was sharp medicine that would cure all his diseases.

Then the executioner hesitated, and Raleigh told him to strike.

He was being killed for a fifteen year old treason conviction that everyone knew was rigged, revived to satisfy the Spanish ambassador over something Raleigh's son had done in South America.

Raleigh's career under Elizabeth I was the Elizabethan age in one man. He put down a Catholic rising in Munster, became Captain of the Queen's Guard in 1587, and worked as a privateer, which is the polite term for a pirate with a royal licence.

In 1591 he secretly married Bess Throckmorton, one of Elizabeth's ladies in waiting, which the Queen regarded as a personal betrayal, and both of them went to the Tower for a month.

He bought his way back with the capture of the Madre de Deus in 1592, a Portuguese carrack whose cargo was worth a staggering amount, and in 1595 he was commissioned to go and find El Dorado.

The main evidence was a confession from Lord Cobham, who retracted it and then re-made it, and Raleigh was denied the right to have Cobham brought into court to face him. The prosecutor Edward Coke abused him from the bench.

Raleigh defended himself so well that the trial started turning public opinion in his favour, which is a rare thing for a man already convicted in everyone's mind.

He was condemned, then reprieved at the last moment, and spent the next thirteen years in the Tower.

And that is where he did the work he should be remembered for. He also kept telling anybody who would listen that there was a gold mine in Guiana.

Palmer Luckey says analysts claiming it's too expensive to manufacture in the US are lying to protect megacorps

"I think I have a more realistic view than almost anybody. One of the problems with all these analysts that are telling you that it's going to cost $37,000 to build an American iPhone or $100,000 to buy an American computer."

"How do I know that? Because I have to make stuff in America every day because I work in the defense industry. The stuff that Anduril makes every day is not actually that different from a computer. My drones are basically computers. They have memory, a GPU, a CPU, sensors, batteries, a rugged integration."

"The only difference between an Anduril attack drone and a laptop is a keyboard and a screen. That is not that hard to figure out, especially for a guy like me who started Oculus an

items.tx:
This is true everywhere in the West.

Palmer Luckey just launched BlueChip with Qualcomm, a laptop designed and assembled in the United States. The "analysts" told us an American computer would cost $100,000. Luckey says it'll cost about 20% more than a high-end PC. The gap between those two numbers is the size of the lie.

In France, we know this song by heart.

Taxis. In 2008, a government commission proposed opening up taxi licenses. Strikes, highways blocked, and the government backed down within days. A Paris taxi license would eventually resell for over €200,000. Scarcity created by the state turned into private wealth. It took Uber to break it, and in 2014 the government passed a law to try to lock it all back down.

Telecom. In 2005, Orange, SFR and Bouygues were fined €534M for colluding on market share. In 2012, a newcomer called Free launched unlimited plans at €19.99. Prices collapsed. Nobody went bankrupt. We had just been paying a cartel.

Pharmacies. A legal monopoly down to the last box of over-the-counter Tylenol. France's largest supermarket chain has been fighting for over fifteen years for the right to sell it. Still no.

Notaries. Decades of de facto caps on the number of practices. When reform finally opened new offices, they took to the streets.

Driving schools. A startup called Ornikar shows up with a cheaper license path, and the industry drags it into court.

And at the EU level, GDPR and the AI Act: rules that only a company with 200 lawyers can comply with. Exactly the moat incumbents dream of.

The pattern is always the same. Manufacture scarcity through law, call it protection, and tell everyone there's no other way.

What AI is doing right now is exposing the scam run by what I call the pseudo-communist entrepreneurs. People who preach free markets and live off administered rents. Central planning, privatized.

The perfect embodiment is Bill Gates. In 2005, he called people who wanted to loosen intellectual property rules "modern-day communists." The irony is total. In the 90s, Microsoft charged PC makers a license fee on every machine they shipped, whether Windows was installed on it or not. The Justice Department had to ban the practice in 1994. Then came the US antitrust ruling for monopoly abuse, then a €497M fine from Brussels in 2004. The real central planner was him.

This whole economy rests on one thing: production costs were high and opaque, so they could charge you for the license, the toll, the stamp. AI is crushing that cost. Code is heading toward zero. Entry-level legal, accounting and medical expertise is heading toward zero. And when producing something costs almost nothing, a rent can no longer be defended by economics, only by law. That's when everyone sees the machinery naked.

It's going to blow up. And it's going to create insane abundance.

Thank you Palmer Luckey for yesterday.

Two days ago I wrote a thread about geniuses. I think Palmer Luckey has the potential to join Elon Musk in that category within a few years. Oculus at 19, Anduril closing in on $100B, and now he's going after the very idea that the West has forgotten how to build things. You see maybe one trajectory like this per generation.
